core: The Chicago School's shift from kinds of people to kinds of places (human ecology, Park's natural areas)
Burgess's concentric zone model and the zone in transition
Shaw and McKay's method: plotting addresses of juvenile-court-referred boys and computing area rates across three Chicago series (1900-1906, 1917-23, 1927-33)
The decisive evidence: high delinquency rates persisted in the same areas across two and three decades even where the nationality composition of the population had turned over completely
The three structural antecedents - low economic status, residential mobility, ethnic heterogeneity - and the mediating mechanism of weakened informal social control
The systemic reformulation: measuring the mediator directly as friendship networks, supervision of teenage peer groups, and organizational participation (Sampson and Groves 1989)
Collective efficacy (Sampson, Raudenbush and Earls 1997): social cohesion among neighbors combined with willingness to intervene on behalf of the common good; the Chicago design and what it found
Evidence status: strong on association, hard on causation because people select into neighborhoods; what the Moving to Opportunity experiment did and did not show
Why 'ethnic heterogeneity' must be read as a historical structural variable confounded with disadvantage and segregation, never as a claim about any group
supporting: Court referrals as an index of delinquency and its limits, acknowledged by Shaw and McKay themselves
Compositional versus contextual explanation, and the ecological fallacy
McKay's 1969 update showing the sharpest increases and the sharpest decreases in delinquency rates both occurred in predominantly Black Chicago communities
Sampson, Morenoff and Raudenbush (2005) on how much of measured racial and ethnic gaps in violence family and neighborhood context accounted for

The general framework of criminological theory and evidence standards, which the what-causes-crime lesson owns
Policing responses to neighborhood conditions: community policing, hot-spots policing, broken-windows enforcement, and police discretion, which the policing lessons own

claims.claim: The Chicago School of the 1920s and 1930s applied human ecology to the city, treating urban areas rather than individual offenders as the unit of analysis; Robert Park described recurring 'natural areas' and Ernest Burgess proposed that the American city tends to expand in concentric zones - Zone I the central business and industrial district, Zone II the 'zone in transition', Zone III workingmen's homes, Zone IV the residential zone, Zone V the outer commuters' zone.

Shaw and McKay measured delinquency as rates of male juveniles referred to the Chicago juvenile court, computed by area for three series - 1900-1906, 1917-23 and 1927-33 - and were explicit that official cases are an index of, not a complete enumeration of, proscribed activity.

The Chicago areas with the highest rates of delinquents clustered in and around the zone in transition, and those same areas carried the invasion of industry and the largest number of condemned buildings, the highest rates of welfare receipt, the lowest median rents and the lowest percentage of family-owned houses, along with the highest rates of infant deaths, tuberculosis and mental illness; Shaw and McKay also computed area rates for commitments, police arrests, truancy and adult crime alongside the juvenile court series.

Of the 25 Chicago areas with the highest delinquency rates in the 1900-1906 series, 19 were among the 25 highest in 1917-23 and 18 among the 25 highest in 1927-33; across the same 106 areas the rate correlations were .85 (plus or minus .04) between 1900-1906 and 1917-23 and .61 (plus or minus .04) between 1900-1906 and 1927-33, even though the nationality composition of the population had changed completely in some of those neighborhoods.

Shaw and McKay concluded from the persistence of area rates through population turnover that race, nativity and nationality are not by themselves vitally related to juvenile delinquency, and that the higher rates recorded for particular groups were closely related to where those groups were concentrated in the city; standardizing for area distribution lowered the Italian rate from 7.06 to 4.29 and the Polish rate from 4.58 to 3.99 while raising the rate for the 'all others' group from 2.94 to 3.23.

In the 1969 revised edition McKay reported that in Chicago the communities with the sharpest relative increases in delinquency rates between the 1934-40 and 1958-61 series (Lawndale, Woodlawn, Englewood) and the communities with comparably sharp decreases (communities 35, 38 and 40) were both predominantly Black, which undercuts any reading of the trend data as a property of a racial group.

The 1969 revised edition's introduction by James F. Short, Jr. notes that later replications found the association between delinquency and foreign-born population absent in Baltimore and Indianapolis and slightly negative in Detroit, so the specific social conditions correlated with delinquency vary with historical period and local structure even where the general pattern of concentrated disadvantage holds.

Sampson and Groves (1989) formulated and gave social disorganization theory its first direct test, hypothesising that low economic status, ethnic heterogeneity, residential mobility and family disruption produce community social disorganization, measured as local friendship networks, control of street-corner teenage peer groups and prevalence of organizational participation; they tested it on 238 British localities from a 1982 survey of 10,905 residents and replicated it on 300 localities and 11,030 residents in 1984, finding that between-community variation in social disorganization transmitted much of the effect of structural characteristics on victimization and offending rates.

Sampson, Raudenbush and Earls (1997) defined collective efficacy as social cohesion among neighbors combined with their willingness to intervene on behalf of the common good, tested it on a 1995 survey of 8,782 residents of 343 Chicago neighborhoods, and found it negatively associated with violence with individual-level characteristics, measurement error and prior violence controlled, and that the associations of concentrated disadvantage and residential instability with violence were largely mediated by collective efficacy.

Collective efficacy is not the same as dense neighborly ties: reviews of the neighborhood-effects literature report that the association between social ties and crime is often mediated by informal social control and cohesion, and that only certain patterns of ties are related to crime, so it is the activation of ties toward shared expectations rather than their sheer density that appears to matter.

Selection bias is described in the neighborhood-effects review literature as probably the biggest challenge facing neighborhood-level research: area differences in an outcome may reflect which families end up in which neighborhoods rather than an effect of the neighborhood, and people appear to select neighborhoods partly on segregation, economic status and friendship ties.

Moving to Opportunity was the first random-assignment social science experiment designed to identify causal effects of moving from high-poverty to lower-poverty neighborhoods; from 1994 to 1998 it enrolled 4,604 low-income households with children living in high-poverty public or assisted housing in Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Los Angeles and New York, and assigned them at random to an experimental group (vouchers usable only in tracts with 1990 poverty below 10 percent, plus mobility counseling), a Section 8 only group (unrestricted vouchers, no special counseling), or a control group.

The MTO final impacts evaluation, 10 to 15 years after random assignment, found sustained improvements in housing quality, neighborhood socioeconomic composition and safety, lower rates of extreme obesity, diabetes, psychological distress and major depression among adults, and no detectable impacts on adult work, earnings or other economic outcomes; it found few statistically significant impacts on educational outcomes and few on risky and criminal behavior, with signs of a gender difference among youth and some indication of reduced drug-selling arrests.

MTO also moved families into neighborhoods where neighbors were more willing to work together to support shared norms, a measure of informal social control, but it did not identify which neighborhood mechanism produced any given outcome, because moving changes bundles of neighborhood variables at once and voucher recipients still chose where to live within the permitted range.

In a Chicago study of 2,974 participants aged 8 to 25 in 180 neighborhoods followed from 1995 to 2002, alongside a community survey of 8,782 residents, the odds of perpetrating violence were 85 percent higher for Black than for White participants and 10 percent lower for Latino than for White participants, and more than 60 percent of the Black-White gap and the entire Latino-White gap were explained primarily by parents' marital status, immigrant generation and dimensions of neighborhood social context.

Social disorganization in the Chicago School sense means the inability of a community's social institutions - family, school, religion, government, economy - to regulate the behavior of its members, not moral disorder or the absence of social life.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether ethnic heterogeneity is a genuine structural cause of weakened social control or an artifact of the segregated, disadvantaged places where heterogeneity was measured.
positions: Shaw and McKay treated a rapidly changing mix of nationalities as a structural obstacle to shared norms and mutual supervision, and Sampson and Groves retained ethnic heterogeneity as an antecedent in the first direct test of the theory.

Later work found the association unstable across cities and periods - the 1969 edition's own introduction records that the delinquency/foreign-born association was absent in Baltimore and Indianapolis and slightly negative in Detroit - and contemporary neighborhood research substitutes concentrated disadvantage and residential instability, which is what collective-efficacy research measured in Chicago.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents ethnic heterogeneity as the historical variable Shaw and McKay measured, states plainly that in American cities it was not separable from poverty and segregation, records that later replications did not reproduce the association, and notes that the modern successor literature uses concentrated disadvantage and residential instability instead. No group is presented as criminogenic; Shaw and McKay's own standardization results and McKay's 1969 trend data are used to show why that reading fails on the theory's own evidence.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strong the causal evidence for neighborhood effects on crime actually is.
positions: Observational neighborhood research finds large, replicated associations between structural disadvantage, low collective efficacy and violence.

Because families are not randomly distributed across neighborhoods, those associations may partly reflect selection; the randomized MTO experiment found real effects on health and safety but no detectable effects on adult earnings or youth educational achievement, and few significant effects on risky and criminal behavior.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the association evidence, states the selection problem, reports MTO's design and its actual findings including the nulls, and notes the review-literature point that even a successful randomization of housing vouchers does not isolate which neighborhood mechanism is doing the work. It draws no policy conclusion in either direction.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether dense social ties in a neighborhood reduce crime.
positions: The systemic reformulation treats friendship networks and organizational participation as the mediating mechanism, and Sampson and Groves found these measures carried much of the structural effect.

Later work found that ties matter mainly when they are activated toward shared expectations, and that some tie patterns show no protective association; collective efficacy was proposed to capture the activation rather than the density.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the systemic reformulation as a real advance and collective efficacy as a refinement of it, and explicitly warns students not to equate 'people know each other' with 'crime is low'.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft made no substantive claim about social disorganization at all: it described the topic as 'a foundational concept in Criminal Justice & Criminology', defined it circularly as 'a foundational Criminal Justice & Criminology concept covered in this lesson', and offered a toolbox-drawer analogy unconnected to neighborhoods, delinquency, or the Chicago School.
The draft's three quick-check questions tested generic study skills ('Defining it and applying it to an example') rather than any content of social disorganization theory.
The draft cited zero sources while asserting that the concept is used 'as a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions'.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with a researched lesson built on Shaw and McKay's own data, Sampson and Groves' first direct test, the 1997 Science collective-efficacy study, the neighborhood-effects review literature, and the HUD MTO final impacts evaluation.

Anchored the persistence finding in the primary source with its actual numbers (25-highest-area overlaps of 19 and 18; correlations of .85 and .61 across 106 areas) instead of the vague textbook version that 'the zones affected all ethnicities'.

Corrected the common misreading that collective efficacy means neighborly friendliness or dense ties, defining it as cohesion plus willingness to intervene for the common good and noting that ties must be activated.

Reported MTO's null results on earnings, education and most criminal behavior alongside its health and safety effects, rather than presenting the experiment as confirming or refuting neighborhood effects.

Reframed 'ethnic heterogeneity' as a historical measured variable, added the confounding-with-segregation critique, added the evidence that later replications did not reproduce the foreign-born association, and used Shaw and McKay's standardization results and McKay's 1969 trend data to foreclose any reading of the theory as a claim about groups.

Sampson and Groves (1989), Sampson, Raudenbush and Earls (1997), Sampson, Morenoff and Gannon-Rowley (2002) and Sampson, Morenoff and Raudenbush (2005) are all commercially published scholarship. Each is REFERENCE_ONLY; only findings, designs and figures are reported.

sourceRecords.title: Community Structure and Crime: Testing Social-Disorganization Theory, American Journal of Sociology 94(4):774-802 (January 1989)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert J. Sampson and W. Byron Groves (University of Chicago Press)
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical DOI registered; the copy actually read on 2026-08-19 was the author-modified abstract and record in the NCJRS Virtual Library at https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/abstracts/community-structure-and-crime-testing-social-disorganization-theory, with bibliographic details confirmed against Crossref. Supports: that Shaw and McKay's theory had never been directly tested before this paper; the four hypothesized antecedents (low economic status, ethnic heterogeneity, residential mobility, family disruption); the three measures of community social organization (local friendship networks, control of street-corner teenage peer groups, organizational participation); the 1982 British Crime Survey test on 238 localities and 10,905 residents and the 1984 replication on 300 localities and 11,030 residents; and the finding that between-community variation in social disorganization transmitted much of the structural effect on victimization and offending.

sourceRecords.title: Neighborhoods and Violent Crime: A Multilevel Study of Collective Efficacy, Science 277(5328):918-924 (15 August 1997)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert J. Sampson, Stephen W. Raudenbush and Felton Earls (American Association for the Advancement of Science)
sourceRecords.notes: Bibliographic record and full published abstract retrieved from the Europe PMC REST API (MED:9252316) on 2026-08-19; the Science full text is paywalled and was not read. Supports the precise definition of collective efficacy as social cohesion among neighbors combined with their willingness to intervene on behalf of the common good; the design (1995 survey of 8,782 residents of 343 Chicago neighborhoods, multilevel analysis); the high between-neighborhood reliability of the measure; the negative association with violence net of individual-level characteristics, measurement error and prior violence; and the finding that associations of concentrated disadvantage and residential instability with violence were largely mediated by collective efficacy.

sourceRecords.title: Assessing 'Neighborhood Effects': Social Processes and New Directions in Research, Annual Review of Sociology 28:443-478 (2002)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert J. Sampson, Jeffrey D. Morenoff and Thomas Gannon-Rowley (Annual Reviews)
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read on 2026-08-19 from a publicly posted PDF of the JSTOR scan (http://dsodown.mywebtext.org/pdf/s01-Sampson_Robert.pdf); canonical DOI registered. Supports: the review's scope of 40-plus peer-reviewed studies from the mid-1990s to 2001; the four classes of neighborhood mechanism and the distinction between social ties/interaction and collective efficacy; the finding that the association of ties with crime is largely mediated by informal social control and cohesion and holds only for certain tie patterns; the statement that selection bias is probably the biggest challenge facing neighborhood-level research and that people select neighborhoods partly on segregation, economic status and friendship ties; and the caution that MTO's randomization of vouchers changes bundles of neighborhood variables at once and does not randomly allocate neighborhood conditions, so it cannot by itself identify the mechanism.

sourceRecords.title: Moving to Opportunity for Fair Housing Demonstration Program: Final Impacts Evaluation - Executive Summary (November 2011)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research

sourceRecords.title: Moving To Opportunity (program overview and reports index)

HUD's own plain-language description of the demonstration: that it was the first random-assignment social science experiment designed to identify the causal effects of moving from high-poverty to lower-poverty neighborhoods, the 1994-1998 enrollment window and five cities, the structure of the two treatment groups and the control group, and HUD's summary that MTO expanded access to neighborhoods where residents felt safer but did not lead to better employment outcomes for adults or grown children nor improve education outcomes for youth. sourceRecords.title: Social Anatomy of Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Violence, American Journal of Public Health 95(2):224-232 (February 2005)
sourceRecords.provider: Robert J. Sampson, Jeffrey D. Morenoff and Stephen Raudenbush (American Public Health Association)
sourceRecords.notes: Published abstract and bibliographic record retrieved from the Europe PMC REST API (MED:15671454) on 2026-08-19; the article is not open access and the full text was not read, so the lesson reports only what the abstract states. Supports the design (three waves of data from 1995 to 2002 on 2,974 participants aged 8 to 25 in 180 Chicago neighborhoods, augmented by a community survey of 8,782 residents) and the reported results (odds of perpetrating violence 85 percent higher for Black than White participants and 10 percent lower for Latino than White participants; more than 60 percent of the Black-White gap and the entire Latino-White gap explained primarily by parents' marital status, immigrant generation and dimensions of neighborhood social context). Used only to show that measured group differences in this study were largely accounted for by family and neighborhood context; no causal claim about any group is made.
